newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia Metals--Zinc downside seen limited after rout.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals--Zinc downside seen limited after rout.

text.p: Any further declines in zinc prices, after a rout on the London Metal Exchange (LME) overnight, are likely to be limited, as zinc demand remains strong relative to supply, Japanese traders said on Wednesday.
They added, however, that uncertainty over the volume of short positions held by Chinese smelters would keep the market nervous.

The LME benchmark three-month zinc price dropped about $300 to a low of $1,370 per tonne in volatile trade on Tuesday, erasing the gains of the past month in the space of an hour as investment funds and other speculators scrambled to liquidate their positions.

"Although the speed of the fall overnight was beyond my expectations, the collapse was a much needed technical correction. Zinc prices may recover to $1,400, and that level may be supported for some time," a trading house trader said.

An official of China National Nonferrous Metals Corp's (CNNC) import and export company said on Wednesday that the sharp fall in zinc prices on the LME was not enough to wipe out losses faced by Chinese smelters that still hold short positions.
Zinc hit a seven year-high of $1,675 on Monday. Traders have said the rally was almost exclusively on the back of China's short positions.
Another Japanese trading house trader said he believed relatively large short positions remained open in the September contract, which would cause further volatility.
Some traders also said a European trader believed to hold massive long positions was trying to lift prices to avoid possible losses.
Traders agreed that another key to market direction was zinc stocks, adding that they would watch to see whether warehouse stocks in Singapore climbed further in the summer.
Japanese zinc premiums, despite firm demand, remained low at around $20 per tonne over LME cash prices, due to pressure from continued robust exports from China at lower levels.
In the aluminium market, premiums weakened slightly as the physical aluminium market has been slow due to a rise in prices on the LME and Japan's firm premiums.
"There's little business in the spot market. The backwardation and the weaker yen have kept end-users out of the market," one senior trader said.
Japan's physical copper market also remained quiet due partly to slow domestic demand.
Copper premiums were unchanged at $50 to $60 per tonne.
"Physical copper business has been slack due partly to the unfavourable weather recently," a copper trader said.
